articles.title: Trisomy 21 Perturbs Oligodendrocyte Developmental States and Oligo-Neuron Communication in Human Forebrain Assembloids
articles.content: Intellectual disability is a hallmark of Down syndrome (DS), caused by the triplication of human chromosome 21. Abnormal neuronal connectivity and impaired myelination are consistently observed in DS, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we used DS-derived isogenic induced pluripotent stem cell-derived forebrain assembloids (FAs) to investigate oligodendrocyte lineage cell (OLLC) development and neuron-glia interactions. Trisomic FAs exhibited an expansion of BCAS1+ pre-myelinating OLLCs, without a corresponding increase in myelin basic protein (MBP) expression. Transcriptomic analyses identified a euploid-enriched, trophic and maturation-supportive state (OLLC_2-TMS) and a trisomy-enriched synaptic interactions and differentiation state (OLLC_3-SID), lacking coordinated enrichment in myelination-promoting programs. Corresponding transcriptional signatures were identified in OLLCs from early postnatal human cortex. Increased excitatory neuronal contacts with pre-myelinating OLLCs accompanied ultrastructural myelin abnormalities in trisomic assembloids. Our findings suggest that trisomy redirects OLLC development toward a pre-myelinating state, uncoupling oligodendrocyte differentiation from productive myelination.

articles.title: Levodopa induced dyskinesia severity is linked to distinct microstructural alterations in nigrostriatal and brainwide neural circuits
articles.content: Dopaminergic replacement therapy via L-DOPA is the major medical therapy for Parkinsons Disease. Long-term L-DOPA administration is known to cause dyskinetic movements, L-DOPA Induced Dyskinesia (LID). It remains unclear if the LID related, maladaptive changes in brain structure/function are localized to neural circuits within the nigrostriatal DA system or have brainwide impact. We employed multi-shell diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and correlational tractography to investigate structural brain networks associated with daily administration of L-DOPA and the development of LID in the unilateral 6-hydroxydopamine rat model. 53% of rats receiving L-DOPA therapy developed severe LID. Tractography found brainwide statistical maps positively and negatively associated with LID severity highlighted by bilateral neural circuits contained in the lesioned nigrostriatal system as well as others including the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex. These results suggest that systemic dysfuntion in brainwide neural circuits forms the mechanistic basis the maladaptive changes underlying LID.

articles.title: An expanded toolbox for genetic access to molecularly defined cortical intratelencephalic neuron subtypes
articles.content: Among the multiple cortical glutamatergic neuron classes, intratelencephalic (IT) neurons represent the largest class and project within the cortex and striatum. IT neurons have been amplified and diversified throughout mammalian evolution and are thought to underlie increasingly complex mammalian cognition. However, despite their diversity and significance in cortical processes, few existing tools connect the molecular signatures to the projection patterns of distinct IT subtypes, limiting our ability to understand their organization and function at a subtype resolution. Here, we illustrate six novel gene knock-in mouse lines based on IT-specific markers, labeling subpopulations with unique cortico-cortical and corticostriatal projection patterns. These include two broad subpopulations with upper-layer (Cux1-Flp) versus lower-layer (Kcnh5-CreER) expression biases, two narrow upper-layer subpopulations with contrasting callosal (Wfs1-Flp) and local (Igfn1-Flp) projection patterns, and two narrow lower-layer subpopulations with contrasting bilateral (Deptor-CreER) versus ipsilateral-predominant (Ptprm-CreER) corticostriatal projection patterns. Upper-layer Wfs1+ and lower-layer Ptprm+ IT neurons also project to perirhinal/ectorhinal cortex with densities that vary across cortical areas. Finally, we use in vivo calcium imaging in mice performing a reach-withdraw-drink task to demonstrate subtype-specific temporal dynamics in upper-layer Wfs1+ versus lower-layer Deptor+ neurons. Our work expands the toolbox of transgenic mice to access molecularly defined IT neuron subpopulations.

articles.title: State-dependent modulation of cross-area sensory processing in mouse neocortex
articles.content: Perception and decision-making rely on distributed cortical circuits that transform sensory inputs into choices and actions. Such cortical processing varies with behavioral state, such that the same inputs can be handled differently across states. However, how behavioral state shapes sensory processing across distributed brain regions remains unclear. To address this question, we trained mice to perform a two-alternative choice task that required discrimination between paired auditory and whisker cues. During task training, we simultaneously recorded neuronal population activity from the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), using two-photon imaging of neurons expressing the fluorescent calcium indicator GCaMP6f. Using a Hidden Markov Model with Generalized Linear Models (GLM-HMM), we identified three latent behavioral states, including one optimal-performing stimulus-guided state and two sub-optimal biased states. We found that the optimal state was associated with stronger sensory representation in S1 and PPC, as well as stronger bottom-up information transfer from S1 to anterior PPC (PPC-A). In contrast, biased states showed weaker sensory coding and relatively stronger involvement of rostrolateral PPC (PPC-RL). State-dependent differences were present in both task-related and task-orthogonal population activity. These results show that internal states modulate not only local sensory encoding, but also the routing of task-relevant information across cortical networks.
articles.author: Han, S., Helmchen, F.

articles.title: HERC1 Loss of Function Causes a Developmental Disorder with Impaired Hippocampal Function
articles.content: Pathogenic variants in HERC1 are associated with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by macrocephaly, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and psychomotor dysfunction. Although genetic and molecular studies suggest a loss-of-function mechanism, definitive in vivo evidence that HERC1 deficiency is sufficient to cause neurodevelopmental abnormalities is lacking. Using a HERC1 knockout mouse model, we investigated the behavioural, neuronal, and synaptic consequences of complete HERC1 loss. HERC1 deficiency caused motor coordination and cognitive deficits in both sexes, while male mutants additionally displayed hyperactivity and increased anxiety-like behaviour. Histological analyses revealed selective hippocampal abnormalities, including disruption of dentate gyrus organization, whereas Purkinje cells survival and cerebellar compartmentalization remained preserved. HERC1-deficient mice exhibited a marked increase in hippocampal GABAergic interneurons, impaired maturation of dendritic spines in CA1 pyramidal neurons, and altered adult neurogenesis, indicating widespread defects in hippocampal circuit organization. Consistent with these structural abnormalities, glutamatergic synaptic components were significantly altered throughout the hippocampus. These molecular changes showed a sex-dependent pattern, with predominantly presynaptic defects in males and postsynaptic alterations in females. Despite these differences, whole-cell recordings revealed a common functional phenotype in both sexes. At both mossy fibre-CA3 and Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses, HERC1-deficient neurons exhibited a progressive inability to sustain excitatory neurotransmission during repetitive stimulation, resulting in impaired steady-state glutamatergic transmission. Together, these findings demonstrate that loss of HERC1 function is sufficient to produce a neurodevelopmental phenotype and identify HERC1 as a critical regulator of hippocampal circuit assembly and function. Our results provide mechanistic insight into the pathogenesis of HERC1-associated disorders and establish the Herc1 knockout mouse as a preclinically relevant model for investigating disease mechanisms and therapeutic approaches.

articles.title: An atlas of the aging glycoproteome reveals how glycosylation modulates autoantibody binding in the brain
articles.content: N-glycosylation generates substantial molecular diversity, yet how glycan composition varies throughout aging remains poorly understood. We mapped the N-glycoproteome of brain, liver, spleen, kidney, and plasma across nine ages spanning the mouse lifespan, identifying 80,618 unique N-glycopeptides at 9,211 glycosites on 4,391 glycoproteins, together with matched proteomic trajectories (glycoproteinatlas.org). Organ identity was the dominant determinant of glycan composition, but numerous glycosites nevertheless underwent remodeling with age. The brain showed a prominent age-associated increase in short paucimannose glycans, driven in part by the age-associated increase in the glycan-processing enzyme HEXB. In white matter, a hotspot for this change, aging increased the paucimannosylation of Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG), a major target of central nervous system autoimmunity. We identified MOG-reactive autoantibodies in aged individuals and patients with MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) and showed that the glycan at MOG N60 modulates autoantibody binding. Experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) recapitulated a subset of the age-associated glycosite changes, revealing shared glycosylation signatures between aging and autoimmune targeting of MOG. Together, these findings reveal site-specific N-glycosylation as both a marker of age and a regulator of molecular interactions.

articles.title: Computational approaches to deep learning–driven EEG analysis for neurological disease diagnosis: a systematic review
articles.content: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a widely used non-invasive neurophysiological technique for analyzing brain dynamics and diagnosing neurological diseases. However, the non-stationary nature, low signal-to-noise ratio, and inter-subject variability of EEG signals cause significant challenges to traditional analytical approaches. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful computational tool for EEG analysis, which enables automated feature learning and improved diagnostic accuracy with minimal human-driven feature extraction. This review systematically explains computational approaches in deep learning-driven EEG analysis for the diagnosis of neurological diseases. It includes recent advances in deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), hybrid configurations, Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Large Language Models (LLM), autoencoders, and transformer-based models, with a focus on their capacity to model spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal dynamics in EEG signals. This is applicable in diagnosing major neurological disorders such as Epilepsy, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Encephalopathy, Parkinson’s disease (PD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), sleep disorders, and developmental brain disorders. Furthermore, we discuss essential preprocessing strategies and denoising techniques, showing how removing biological artifacts prevents diagnostic models from confusing noise with actual signs of disease. Key challenges such as limited data availability, lack of model interpretability, inter-subject variability, and difficulty in clinical translation are identified and critically discussed. Finally, key emerging trends and future research directions are identified to support the development of clinical applications of EEG-based disease diagnostic systems.

articles.title: Implementing the ILAE 2025 seizure taxonomy in medical software
articles.content: The International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE), working via a multidisciplinary task force, has issued a position paper with updated seizure classification guidelines (2025) replacing its previous guidance (2017), establishing a revised de-facto standard for clinical assessment and classification of epileptic seizures. The 2025 model simplifies the system, making it easier to adopt in different clinical settings while also clarifying the taxonomic rules, the definition of consciousness, and the application of phenomena-based descriptors. As a result, clinical practitioners, technologists, and medical software developers also face the challenge of adopting the new standard in their applications and workflows. To aid in the realization of this update in medical device software, this article presents a proposed numerical structure for ILAE 2025 edition of the seizure classification system as a definition of interacting bitfields, establishing an open reference implementation to support common storage and interoperability between software environments. Assigning each orthogonal concept to a single bit, we encode the core ontology and expanded descriptor set so that they fit into 32-bit and 128-bit unsigned integers, respectively. TypeScript, known for its expressiveness and practical applicability, is used as the implementation language for these definitions. Examples are provided to help implementers incorporate the proposed specification into their software, as well guidance for mapping from the ILAE 2017 type system to the updated ILAE 2025 type system. The reference specification, with test cases and examples, is maintained in a public code repository and available under a permissive license.
articles.author: Jukka Peltola

articles.title: Cross-modal alignment with language tokens for unified multilingual image-to-text generation
articles.content: Current multimodal translation systems typically employ a cascaded pipeline where image captioning and machine translation are performed sequentially, leading to error propagation and semantic drift. This paper introduces a unified neural architecture that integrates visual encoding, English caption generation and multilingual translation into a single end-to-end model. Our first key contribution is this unified framework which jointly optimizes both tasks through shared latent representations enabling richer cross-modal learning and more semantically consistent multilingual outputs than conventional systems. The architecture incorporates two core technical innovations. First, we introduce a cross-modal representation alignment mechanism that directly fuses hierarchical visual features from a CNN encoder with multilingual linguistic embeddings in the Transformer decoder. This ensures visual semantics (e.g., gender, count, and object attributes) are preserved during translation effectively grounding multilingual outputs in the visual context and rectifying a common failure mode of text-only NMT. Second, we design a language token driven conditioning strategy prepending learnable target language tokens to guide a single multilingual model. This allows dynamic adaptation to diverse syntax and morphology without requiring separate decoders for each language. Empirical evaluations on MS COCO and OPUS multilingual datasets demonstrate notable improvements over existing multimodal and cascaded baselines achieving a BLEU-4 score of 44.8 for English captioning and an average BLEU of 41.1 across five target languages (Chinese, French, Arabic, Spanish, and Hindi), representing gains of 2.2 and 2.0 points, respectively, over cascaded baselines. COMET scores averaging 0.732 further confirm the semantic fidelity of our visually grounded translations. The proposed framework establishes a scalable, visually grounded and linguistically adaptive solution for multilingual caption generation contributing a meaningful advancement toward integrated vision-language translation research and real-world accessibility applications.
